activities.description: The narrator introduces the topic of the outer planets.
A diagram of the solar system with the sun and all eight planets appears.

activities.description: The narrator asks a question about which gas giants have rings.
A pause button appears.
Stylized illustrations of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, all with rings, appear.
The narrator reveals that all four gas giants have rings.
The illustrations of Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune disappear.
The narrator explains that only Saturn's rings are visible from Earth.
The illustration of Saturn is incorporated into a diagram of the solar system with all eight planets.

scenes.contextualRelevance: This scene explores the visibility and characteristics of rings.

narrativeProgression.description: This scene explores the topic of rings around gas giants.
The narrator reveals that all gas giants have rings, but only Saturn's are visible from Earth.

scenes.thematicElements: Visibility and characteristics of planetary rings
scenes.title: Gas giant rings

videoEditingDetails.description: Calm, electronic music continues to play.
Smooth animation of planet illustrations appearing and disappearing.

activities.description: The narrator introduces a mnemonic for remembering the order of the planets.
The mnemonic, 'My Very Elegant Mother Always Jumps Sideways Under Neat Pillows,' appears on screen.
Pluto is highlighted and labeled.
The narrator explains that Pluto is not a true planet.
The text 'Dwarf Planet' appears below Pluto.
The narrator lists the rules for a celestial body to be considered a planet.
Text bullets with the three rules appear on screen: 'You must be in orbit around the sun.'
Text bullets with the three rules appear on screen: 'You must be heavy enough to be almost spherical in shape.'
Text bullets with the three rules appear on screen: 'You have cleared your neighbourhood of rocks and debris.'
Pluto is shown orbiting the sun, surrounded by many rocks and debris.
The text 'Pluto' appears next to the illustration.
The narrator explains that Pluto joins other dwarf planets.
An illustration of the dwarf planet Ceres appears, also surrounded by rocks and debris.
The text 'Ceres' appears next to the illustration.

scenes.contextualRelevance: This scene explains celestial classification, focusing on Pluto's status.

narrativeProgression.description: This scene explains the reclassification of Pluto as a dwarf planet and the rules for classifying planets.
The three rules for a celestial body to be considered a planet are outlined.
The narrator explains that other dwarf planets are being discovered.

scenes.thematicElements: Classification of celestial bodies, Pluto's status
scenes.title: Pluto and Dwarf Planets

videoEditingDetails.description: Calm, electronic music continues to play.
Smooth animation of text and illustrations appearing.

activities.description: The narrator defines a moon as a natural satellite orbiting a planet.
A diagram appears showing the Earth orbiting the Sun, with the Moon orbiting the Earth.
The narrator mentions that some planets have many moons while others have none.
A pause button appears.
The text 'Earth' appears above the Earth illustration.
The text 'Moon' appears above the Moon illustration.
The narrator explains that Earth is unusual because its moon is large compared to the planet it orbits.
The narrator explains a theory of the Moon's formation through a large collision early in Earth's history.
An animation depicts the collision theory, showing a large object colliding with the early Earth, ejecting debris that coalesces into the Moon.
The text 'Collision' appears above the animation.
The text 'Captured in orbit' appears below the final stage of the Moon formation animation.
The narrator introduces comets.
The text 'Comets' appears above an illustration of a comet with a tail.
The Boy appears, pointing at the comet.
The narrator explains that people once thought comets were a bad omen.
The comet disappears and the Boy looks up at the night sky.
A diagram of the solar system appears with an elliptical orbit labeled 'Comet orbit.'
The narrator explains that comets are like large dirty snowballs with elliptical orbits.
The narrator explains that some comets take decades, centuries, or longer to complete an orbit.
The narrator mentions Sir Edmund Halley and Halley's Comet.
The text 'Halley's comet' appears next to the comet's orbit in the diagram.
The narrator states that Halley's Comet returns every 75 years and was last seen in 1986.
The narrator explains that comets become visible when their orbit brings them close to the sun.
The diagram now shows the words 'Comet', 'Sun', and 'Earth' next to their respective illustrations.
The narrator explains that the comet's tail always points away from the Sun due to solar wind.
The comet's tail is shown pointing away from the Sun as it moves along its orbit.

trimmingSuggestions.description: The infographic sections for each outer planet could be shortened. While informative, they slow down the pace of the video. A faster transition between key facts for each planet could maintain viewer engagement.
The 'Rules to be a Planet' section could be condensed. The text bullets remain on screen for a long duration, and a faster delivery of the information would make the scene more dynamic.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: This video looks at the characteristics of the outer planets, dwarf planets, moons and
comets.
To see the review of the inner planets, watch this video.
The common feature of the outer planets is that they are all gas giants.
They have no solid surface.
What we observe is a ball of gas or vapor so we cannot land on them.
There is a lot to take in, so you may want to pause the video to have a good read.
Which of the gas giants has rings?
Pause the video while you think of an answer.
The answer is that all four of them have rings, but only those of Saturn are visible from
the Earth.
Until 2006, a verse to recall the planetary order could have been, my very elegant mother
always jumps sideways underneath pillows.
In that year, it was decided that Pluto was not a true planet, and so was reclassified
as a dwarf planet.
Poor Pluto.
There are certain rules to be a planet.
Firstly, you must be in orbit around the sun.
Secondly, you must be heavy enough to be almost spherical in shape.
And thirdly, you have cleared your neighbourhood of rocks and debris.
Pluto joined other named dwarf planets, which are bodies that orbit a star and have a stable
shape, but have not cleared their orbits of other debris.
The large asteroid, Seris, is another example of a dwarf planet and others well beyond Pluto
are being discovered.
A moon is a natural satellite.
It's a body which orbits a planet, and so of course is part of the solar system.
As you will have seen, some of the planets have a large number of moons, and some none
at all.
Stop the video if you want to go back and look.
Earth is unusual, as our moon, the moon, is large when compared to the planet in orbits.
It is thought that the moon was created very early on in the life of the Earth after a
significant interplanetary collision which ejected rock which was then captured in orbit.
There are other objects that are part of our solar system we rarely see.
Comments
People once thought the appearance of a comet in the night sky was a warning of a tragic
event about to happen.
Comments are similar to large dirty snowballs, a few tens of kilometres across.
That follow a huge elliptical path around the sun that may take decades, centuries, or
longer to complete one orbit.
It was Sir Edmund Haley who was first to successfully predict a return of a comet that now bears
his name.
It returns every 75 years, and was last seen in 1986.
You do the maths.
These ancient objects only become visible when their orbit brings them near to the sun.
That's when a huge tale of vaporised material is lit up by sunlight.
Notice that the tail always points away from the sun as it passes by, showing the effect
of the invisible solar wind leaving the surface of the star.
Before you go, did you remember the verse to recall the order of the planets?
